Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Leo was twenty-six when the physical blows from his partner stopped, but the world never quite settled back into place. The attacks had been sudden and heavy: a backhand across the newsroom desk during a deadline, a knee driven into his ribs when he tried to step away, a grip on his wrist that did not loosen until he went still. He had come to believe that harm could arrive without warning, and that people simply could not be trusted. What frightened him most was the lingering sense that he had failed to read the room, that he had said or done something wrong to invite the violence. He spent the months after they parted dwelling on those moments, replaying his own stumbles in his mind, convinced that his inadequacy was the quiet reason the pain kept coming. The first weeks were marked by a restless body and a mind that refused to let the past stay buried. Leo would wake during the night, sheets tangled, lying perfectly still to listen for footsteps or the creak of the floorboards, checking whether he was safe. Even when his mother called to say the apartment was secure and the locks held, he found it impossible to believe her. He was certain that the danger had only paused. The memory of the attacks rarely arrived as a distant recollection. Instead, it would press into his present without transition: the heat of a palm against his collarbone, the sharp twist of a shoulder, the exact ache in his ribs that mirrored the bruises of those years. When the sensation rose, the emotion would overwhelm him so completely that he had to stop what he was doing, pressing his hands flat against the desk or the steering wheel until the wave receded. As a journalist, Leo spent his days moving through spaces that now felt charged. He covered local beats, filing stories from cafés and community centers, but his routes increasingly narrowed. Riding the bus had become a daily trial. The doors would close with a mechanical thud, the vehicle would lurch forward, and Leo would find himself bracing against the sudden movements, his eyes fixed on the mirrors, tracking every shift of the other passengers. Being alone with men proved just as difficult. In his newsroom, when a male editor or a source sat across from him, Leo would feel the familiar tension coil in his jaw. He watched their hands, measured their tone, and waited for the shift. He never allowed himself to feel or express the anger that rose in those moments; instead, he let it settle into his bones, keeping his voice low and his posture guarded. To steady himself, he began to avoid eating or restrict his portions, treating hunger as a way to lighten his body and quiet the internal static. Delays began to carry a quiet threat. When a train held at a signal, when a meeting ran five minutes past its scheduled end, when a text message took too long to arrive, Leo would assume that something bad was happening. The uncertainty itself felt like a warning. Over the months, these habits accumulated. He declined casual dinners when a man might attend, skipped lunch more often than he would admit, and found himself apologizing for small inconveniences, as though his presence were a burden. His relationship, though steady, grew quiet; his partner’s reassurances were met with a polite nod rather than relief, because Leo had come to trust his own vigilance more than anyone else’s promises. What finally brought Leo to seek help was a Tuesday morning in the newsroom. He had been waiting for a source to arrive, and when the clock ticked past the expected minute, the familiar tightness seized his chest. He stepped into the elevator, doors closing behind him, and found himself alone with a male photographer. The metal walls felt too close, the air too warm. He could feel the phantom pressure of his partner’s hands, the exact soreness in his ribs, and the quiet certainty that he was responsible for keeping the threat at bay. He realized he was no longer living in his life so much as monitoring it. He wants to know whether the world can truly be safe, and he hopes to stop carrying the weight of every unspoken danger on his own shoulders.
